Last June I made myself one promise: one Python course, start to finish, no switching. I'm Manoj, and before that summer I had bookmarked eleven courses and completed zero.
I picked a free beginner course with thirty short lessons and stuck a sheet on my cupboard with thirty boxes. One lesson, one box. Around lesson twelve, Dilnaz sent me a course on building apps. She said it was much cooler. I wanted it badly. I wrote its title on the back of my sheet instead and kept going.
The loops lesson took me three evenings, so the thirty boxes took thirty-two days. The day after the last box, I still didn't open anything new. I wrote a tiny program that quizzes my little brother on spellings. Only after it worked did I click Dilnaz's link.

Elizabeth's plan fit on one sticky note: ten questions, a score at the end, classmates can play. The science quiz club at her school in Pune met every Thursday, and Jahnavi, the club secretary, was tired of reading questions aloud from paper.
Elizabeth didn't start a course. At the small desk in the corner of the family flat, she opened a blank file and wrote what she needed first: a way to ask a question. She searched how to take input, tried it, and it worked. Storing ten questions meant lists, so she looked those up next. Repeating the asking needed a loop; that cost an evening of errors and one short explainer video.
By Wednesday night the quiz ran on the club laptop. On Thursday, Jahnavi played first, scored seven, and demanded a rematch. Four more members tried it before the bell.

Coding club note, Tuesday
In September Anirban told me he had finished forty hours of programming videos. He can name every topic: loops, functions, lists. Today I gave the group an empty editor and one task: print the numbers one to ten, then only the even ones.
Tarun finished in four minutes after two wrong tries. Anirban sat very still, then opened a video in another tab. I asked him to close it. For ten minutes he typed and deleted the same line. Finally he said quietly, “In the videos it just works. I always typed what they typed.”
That is the gap. Watching felt like learning, but he never had to produce code from nothing. I did not push it in front of the group. After club we agreed on one small exercise a day, written before any video, and he will show me on Thursday.
– Club mentor

qa.q: What task did the club mentor give the group?
qa.a: Print the numbers one to ten, then only the even ones, in an empty editor.

qa.q: What was Anirban probably feeling while typing and deleting the same line?
qa.a: He was likely embarrassed and confused, since forty hours of videos had made him feel ready and now nothing came out on his own.

qa.q: What could Anirban try instead of more videos?
qa.a: Write one small exercise a day before watching anything and use a video only to get unstuck, so the typing comes from his own thinking.

qa.q: How might Tarun see Anirban's struggle?
qa.a: Tarun might be surprised, since Anirban can name every topic, and may realise that Tarun's own two wrong tries were part of the learning.

grounding: Shows the cost of tutorial hopping without practice: a student who watched many videos cannot write a simple loop in an empty editor.

Saturday night
Worst evening. Chetan bhaiya came home from his hostel and I bragged that I've been learning to code for two months. Which is true, I've watched maybe sixty videos. He opened his laptop, made a new empty file and said, “Write something that counts the words in this sentence. Any way you like.”
I stared. I knew the words “split” and “loop” from videos. I didn't know where to put them. In every video someone else typed first and I copied. Here nobody typed first.
Chetan bhaiya didn't laugh. He said, “Watching isn't the same muscle.” He showed me nothing, just asked me to try one line and run it. It broke. The second line broke too. After forty minutes it counted the words. Forty minutes for four lines.
Tomorrow: no videos until I've written something myself.
– Kiran

qa.a: Something that counts the words in the sentence, any way Kiran liked.

The crash came at eleven at night, the evening before I'd promised Pallavi the timetable maker. I'm Sharmila, and back then my first instinct was to change random lines until something worked.
That night I made myself read the red text instead. The first line named the part called make_slots. The next gave line forty-two. The last said a list index was out of range. So, I thought, something is asking for a slot that doesn't exist. But which part feeds it?
I put a hash in front of every line in the bottom half so it wouldn't run. No crash. The problem lived in that half. I brought it back a few lines at a time, running after each. It broke when the Saturday part returned: I'd given Saturday four periods, but its list only had three. One fix, one run, and it worked. I remember feeling almost calm, which surprised me.

qa.q: What did the last line of the error say?
qa.a: It said a list index was out of range.

qa.q: How did Sharmila feel once the fix worked, and why was that a surprise?
qa.a: Sharmila felt almost calm, which was surprising, since the old habit under late-night pressure was changing random lines in a panic.

qa.q: What else could Sharmila do if hiding half the code had not explained the crash?
qa.a: Add print lines that show what each list holds just before the crash, so the real values reveal which assumption is wrong.

qa.q: How is Pallavi affected by the way Sharmila handled the crash?
qa.a: Pallavi gets the timetable maker on time and working, instead of a rushed version patched with random changes that might break again.

grounding: Shows a teen's reasoning while debugging: reading the error, switching off half the code to find the fault, then fixing and rechecking one change at a time.

Computer club observation, Friday
Imran's weather logger crashed three times before the break. Last month he would have called me over at once. Today I stayed at my desk and listened, because he was talking it through with Harsha, who sits beside him.
“Okay, it says ‘cannot convert string to number’. So somewhere I'm doing maths on text.” He scrolled to the line the message named. “That's the average. So the temperatures are text. Where do they come from?” He hid the averaging part with comment marks and printed the list instead. The numbers came out wrapped in quote marks. “There. They come in from the file as words.” He changed one line to convert them, ran it, then checked the average by hand on Harsha's calculator.
Next step for me: ask Imran to show this method to the Monday beginners.

qa.a: It said "cannot convert string to number".

qa.a: Having Imran walk the Monday beginners through reading one real error and isolating it would show them a method, not just a fix.

qa.a: Harsha hears the reasoning step by step and even helps check the average, so the crash becomes a shared lesson rather than a private struggle.

The community library's wifi was slow, but it was free, and it didn't run out on the twentieth of the month like the data on the family phone. Nilesh sat at the corner table beside Ankita, who volunteered at the desk on Saturdays.
“So here's my thinking,” Nilesh said, opening a notebook. “Home has one laptop, and Didi needs it for her college work till eight. The phone data is shared by five of us. So I can't stream lessons at home, and I can't code whenever I want.”
“So?”
“So every Saturday I download that week's four lessons here. At home I code offline from eight to nine-thirty, because that slot is mine. If I get stuck, I write the question down and bring it here next Saturday.”
Ankita slid the wifi card across. “Four lessons will fit if you start the downloads now.”

Friday
Third Friday of the plan and I nearly skipped it. The deal Maria, Sunny and I made: one problem a week from the practice site, everyone solves it alone, and on Friday after school we each show our solution on Maria's tablet in the library, five minutes each.
This week's problem was about reversing words. I left it till Thursday night and got stuck. I was going to text them that I was ill. Then Maria messaged, “Tejas, you alive? Friday! 🙂” Annoying. But it worked.
I showed my half-solution anyway. Sunny had done it a totally different way, with a loop running backwards. Maria's was the shortest. I felt a bit resentful that both of them finished, but seeing three ways to solve one thing taught me more than a whole video.
Next week's problem is already copied into my notebook.

I'm Vinita, Francis's neighbour across the corridor. For most of October, whenever I passed his open door, he was on the bed with his laptop, earphones in, some coding video playing, nodding along.
One evening he knocked and asked to borrow my old maths notebook, the one with squared pages. He'd drawn a table on the first page with three columns: “week”, “what I did”, “what I can now do without help”. The last column was nearly empty for all three weeks.
After that, things looked different from the corridor. The earphones were out. A small exercise book lay open beside the laptop, and he'd type, groan, type again. A video came on only now and then, for a few minutes, then went off.
Last Sunday he showed me a program that guessed my birthday month in four questions. I don't know exactly what changed in his head. But something did.

qa.a: Week, what I did, and what I can now do without help.

qa.a: Trying a small exercise first and opening a video only when stuck, because it shows gaps right away instead of after three weeks.

qa.a: To Vinita it looks like a switch from quiet nodding to active struggle, groaning and typing, which ends in a program that actually works.

I'm Pradeep. I share a bench with Dilnaz in the computer lab, so I saw most of it. On Monday her drawing program kept filling the whole screen blue instead of drawing a square. She tried things for a while, then stopped and opened a notebook instead of the forum.
She wrote three headings: “What I expected”, “What happened”, “What I tried”. Under the last one she listed four things, including “changed the colour value” and “restarted”. Then she copied only the six lines of code that mattered, not the whole file, and posted all of it on a learner forum.
I told her nobody answers kids. By Tuesday lunchtime someone had replied: she was filling the background inside the loop instead of once before it. She moved one line, and the square appeared. She looked pleased, though all she said was, “Told you.”

qa.q: What were the three headings Dilnaz wrote?
qa.a: What I expected, what happened, and what I tried.

qa.q: How might Dilnaz have felt when the square appeared, and what hints at it?
qa.a: She seemed pleased and a little vindicated; the account notes her look and her short "Told you." 😊

qa.q: What else could Dilnaz do if the forum stayed silent?
qa.a: Take the same three-part write-up to the computer teacher, since a well-formed question works in person too.

qa.q: How does the episode change Pradeep's view of asking online?
qa.a: Pradeep expected no one to answer, but a quick reply to a clear question shows that how you ask matters.

grounding: A lab benchmate sees a teen write what she expected, what happened and what she tried, post it on a learner forum, and get a fix within a day.

Thursday: Rashmi's recipe-sharing page won't save anything when she presses the button. She posts on a learner forum: “my code doesn't work pls help”. By night there is one reply: “Doesn't work how?”
Friday: Her uncle Jagdish, who repairs computers at a shop in Nagpur, reads the post over her shoulder. “Could you answer that if a stranger sent it to you?” She rewrites it: what she expected (the recipe appears on the list), what happened (the page reloads and the list stays empty), what she tried (checked spellings, cleared the browser, tested a second recipe). She pastes the twelve lines of the form, not all three hundred.
Saturday morning: Two replies. The second points out that the button reloads the page before saving. She adds one line, and her aloo paratha recipe appears on the list.

qa.q: What did Rashmi's first forum post say?
qa.a: "My code doesn't work pls help".

qa.q: What might Rashmi have felt on Thursday night seeing the one-line reply?
qa.a: Rashmi was probably frustrated and a bit embarrassed, since the reply showed the question gave helpers nothing to work with.

qa.q: What else could Rashmi try while waiting for replies?
qa.a: Test smaller pieces, such as whether the button runs any code at all, which may reveal the fault and sharpen the question further.

qa.q: How might Jagdish feel seeing the Saturday fix?
qa.a: Jagdish is likely proud, because one question from him led Rashmi to a method that works without his help.

grounding: Shows a teen rewriting a vague bug post into what she expected, what happened and what she tried, and getting a useful answer within a day.
